stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Turning point | What changed |
| 1754 | Seven Years' War begins in North America | Britain and France fight for the continent; the colonies are drawn into an imperial war |
| 1763 | Treaty of Paris ends the war | France loses Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi; Britain takes on a huge war debt |
| 1763 | Proclamation of 1763 | Settlement west of the Appalachians is forbidden; the age of salutary neglect ends |
| 1765–1773 | Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Boston Tea Party | Parliament taxes the colonies for revenue; colonists resist, then organize |
| 1776 | Declaration of Independence | The colonies break with Britain and claim government rests on the consent of the governed |
| 1783 | Treaty of Paris ends the Revolution | Britain recognizes American independence; the new nation holds the land to the Mississippi |
| 1787–1789 | Constitution written and ratified | The weak Articles give way to a stronger federal government |
| 1800 | Election of Thomas Jefferson | Power passes peacefully from one party to another for the first time |

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books; stem and options rewritten from fresh-written survivor original-u3-gapfill-mercantilism-02
stem: Throughout the period 1754–1800, British officials defended mercantilist policies such as the Navigation Acts as necessary for the empire. Which of the following best describes the continuity in British economic thinking across this period?

options.text: Britain continued to treat the colonies mainly as suppliers of raw materials and buyers of British manufactured goods.
After 1763 Britain abandoned all restrictions on colonial trade and embraced complete free trade with the colonies.
options.misconception: Britain tightened trade enforcement after 1763 rather than loosening it.

options.text: After the American Revolution, Britain shifted to taxing only goods that its former colonies imported from France.
options.misconception: Britain had no power to tax the independent United States after 1783.

options.text: By the time of the Constitutional Convention in 1787, Britain had given the former colonial assemblies full control over imperial trade policy.
options.misconception: After independence there were no colonial assemblies under British rule to receive such power.

rationales.A: The specific taxes changed — the Sugar Act, the Stamp Act, the Townshend duties — but the underlying mercantilist assumption never did: colonies existed to serve the mother country's economy. Background: the Navigation Acts and the later revenue measures all rested on that same logic throughout the period. That continuity is why colonists protested not just the taxes but Parliament's claimed right to regulate colonial economic life at all.
rationales.B: Britain tightened trade enforcement after 1763 rather than loosening it.
rationales.C: Britain had no power to tax the independent United States after 1783.
rationales.D: After independence there were no colonial assemblies under British rule to receive such power.
rationales.general:
1. Look for what stays the same. The table shows new taxes in 1764, 1765, and 1767 — but the idea behind them never changes.
2. Name the idea. Mercantilism: the colonies exist to feed the mother country's trade, sending raw materials out and buying finished goods back.
3. Check the options. Only one describes a policy that runs through the whole period, from the Navigation Acts to the Townshend duties.
4. Put it together. The taxes were new; the thinking behind them was old.
Remember: when the policy changes but the principle doesn't, the principle is the continuity.
